title: Breaking and Entering: Daniel Avery Returns With a Tremor
transcript:
Daniel Avery began DJing as a teenager at a local indie club night, sort of spanning everything from electro clash to post-punk and first began sort of producing and DJing back in 2009 under the name Stopmakingme, collaborating with artists like Hercules and Love Affair and Metronomy as well and regularly performing at the Iconic Fabric Club in London.

He then went on to be taken under the wing of producers like Erol Alkan and also Andrew Weatherall, who Daniel Avery speaks more about in this interview, Weatherall's legacy and what he gleaned from the late great man.

Since releasing his debut record, Drone Logic, back in 2013, Daniel has gone on to collaborate with numerous artists, including Kelly Lee Owens, Jonny Greenwood from Radiohead and he also released a collaborative album with Alessandro Cortini from Nine Inch Nails back in 2020.

He's really known for his sort of left field electronic production, but his latest album, Tremors, or Tremors, sorry, sees Daniel returning to his roots somewhat, playing in shoegaze bands as a teenager.

He sort of cited early guitar music like Nine Inch Nails and the Deftones and My Bloody Valentine as a really huge formative musical influences for him.

He's, as I mentioned, got quite a few Australian connections here as well with HTRK and we began the interview talking about HTRK.

Apparently, they're one of Daniel Avery's favourite bands of all time.

So, we begin the interview by asking Daniel to tell us about what HTRK's music means to him.

Easily one of my favourite bands of all time.

I discovered him when I just moved to London.

So, for me, they really soundtracked that sort of hazy, those early days, like, into the London nightlife as a youngster.

My comparison is I always think that if the Velvet Underground and Nico were making records now, they might sound a bit like HTRK.

And I mean that as the biggest compliment.

It was such a dream working with Jonnine on that track.

I love her.

And you name-checked HTRK recently as one of your favourite shoegaze artists, perfect for a post-rave come down, as well as another Australian actor who are actually going to be joining me on the show in a couple of weeks, Acopia.

Just really great to see them doing so well on the world stage at the moment.

How did you discover Acopia?

A friend of mine, Palms Trax, a DJ, re-released their debut record and asked me to do a remix.

And I just fell in love with them straight away.

And, yeah, there's just so much great music of that variety coming out of Australia, particularly Melbourne.

I don't know what you have in the water there, but something about that real Broken Beauty shoegaze with loads of pop hooks in it.

I love it.

If you're a shoegaze fan and being from the UK, I don't know if you've seen Simon Reynolds.

He's got a new shoegaze book coming out.

I have it.

I have it.

I have it.

They sent me an early copy, yeah.

Amazing.

Yeah, yeah.

Worth reading, I imagine, his incredible Simon Reynolds.

It's really good.

It's a really interesting read because he always talks about how this is a book that he's wanted to write for a long time because he was right in the heart of that scene.

And so it's as much about being a music fan as, you know, just a music historian.

So, yeah, it's really cool.

Well, congratulations on the new record Tremors, the deluxe version of which has just come out recently with some new remixes as well.

I guess, yeah, you're known for your otherworldly kind of club bangers and your left field production.

But before all of that, like going back to Daniel Avery, the teenager, you were playing in shoegaze bands and I understand worshipping at the altar of guitar bands like the Deftones and Nine Inch Nails and My Bloody Valentine.

And does the new record and I guess the new live shows you've coming up with these full band shows, does it feel like a return to your roots in a way?

It does.

It feels like a sort of full circle moment, but at the same time, I never want it to feel like a sort of throwback or anything.

So the album, the music and the live shows have all of the techno elements that I've picked up along the way over the years.

It's a real mixture of everything that has sort of shaped me over the years.

It's interesting to me because a few people have said, well, if this was where you began, why haven't you done it before?

And I don't have a great answer other than I just don't think I could have done it.

For whatever reason, I'm feeling a certain level of freedom at the moment and I feel as if it's taken this long to sort of incubate the idea.

And here we are.

[Unclear audio at 00:04:49–00:05:22]

We mentioned Nine Inch Nails just before and you released that collaboration.

You've got a great record with Nine Inch Nails since savant Alessandro Cortini back in 2020 called Illusion of Time.

Was that like another full circle moment for you getting to work with one of your heroes in that way?

Absolutely.

Yeah, absolutely.

And still one of my favourite things I've done.

And yeah, so proud of it.

I was actually just talking about that record yesterday with someone.

It came out just at the very, by complete chance, came out at the very beginning of Lockdown.

And it sort of soundtracked that time for a few people, I've been told.

It definitely did for me.

Those weird times of being shut away, I think it offered some kind of solace.

So yeah, I feel really proud of that one.

I was chatting to the founders of Melbourne Electronic Sound Studio, MESS.

I don't know if you're familiar with their work, but Alessandro visited when he was here last time.

They've got this massive collection of rare synthesizers that you can play.

And apparently Alessandro was very hard to impress.

He already sort of had most of them in his personal collection and in his studio.

But they had one, the VCS1, that they've only made three of these synths.

And they've got one there that you can play.

And apparently Alessandro sort of went a bit quiet when he saw that synth in their collection.

I bet.

I bet, yeah.

Are you into synths?

Like are you a bit of a gearhead?

Not as much as those guys.

I really like old machines, but I also really like modern techniques and I use a lot of stuff within the laptop.

And, you know, at the same time, I really like live instrumentation as well.

I always have done, but I've just pushed that forward on the new record.

I like the spaces where all of those things intersect.

I don't feel like a purist in any way.

You know, I like using everything I have in front of me.

Your studio setup sounds pretty amazing too.

It's still in that shipping container by the river Thames in London.

I've been there since the beginning, really.

I've been there since 2012.

It sounds like a pretty, yeah, special space for you.

Can you describe the space?

Because you do a lot of sort of recordings of atmosphere around there too, don't you?

Yeah, that's correct.

The space is only tiny.

It's a shipping container.

So, you know, it's a little metal box.

But it's the surrounding area that's important to me.

It's, you're right in the middle of London, but you're also by the water.

And you're, it feels really serene and quiet and it's not the easiest spot to get to, which I really like, which I really like and sort of tucked away in this little corner and also surrounded by other great musicians and artists.

And there's an illustration school down there and a dance school.

And it's kind of this weird little special corner of London that I feel so lucky to be a part of.

I think this, I always say that I think the sound of my music is often trying to find the space between the sort of madness of the, of the nightclub and the road and the quiet times away from it.

And I think the marriage of those two is what kind of influences so much of what I did.

You've also spoken a lot about like the warmth of distortion and almost wanting to set things on fire.

Not literally, but describing that sort of feeling, the transcendental beauty of noise is something else you've talked about.

Are these concepts like you're often thinking about?

Like what kind of emotions were you chasing on this new record?

Yeah.

I've always loved heavy music in lots of forms and I've always found it really comforting and warm and inviting.

It's just, I don't know what, it must just be how my brain is wired because I feel the same way about a lot of, you know, I like quite dark films and I find a certain comfort in them.

I kind of, I kind of, I was always drawn to like the more shadowy end of, of everything really, films, books, music.

I just find that comfort.

Again, I don't know why exactly, but I do love when it comes to music.

I love the idea of beauty being hidden beneath distortion or noise surrounding a really, like a hook.

No, I just, I just really, I really love it.

I find it warm and inviting.

You also talked previously about the listening phase of an album for you and how listening to music when you're moving can be this totally different experience.

Do you find that, yeah, you absorb the music differently when you're listening and you're moving at the same time?

I think it's my favourite way to do it, actually.

I guess just because I'm travelling so much, but it must have something to do with this idea of companionship and you're never alone when you have music.

I've always really loved that idea and I'm often on my own travelling, physically, but if I have a record in my ears, in my mind, then it's a different experience and, and that can be really heavy, sort of enveloping music.

Um, I just really do enjoy that when I'm listening to other records and yeah, it is often the final test of my own stuff, is, is travelling with, with it, yeah.

[Unclear audio at 00:11:12–00:11:58]

Earlier on in your career, I guess you were taken under the wing of mentors like Erol Alkan and of course the late, great Andrew Weatherall as well.

Both, I guess, were renowned for bridging those worlds of rock and, and dance music.

Only if you felt comfortable, I'd love to talk to you about your relationship with Andrew Weatherall, of course you put out that tribute track for him.

How would you describe Andrew's legacy and I guess as a mentor, what did he teach you?

Well, there are a few things to say here. From afar, before I ever met him, much like Erol, I was really drawn to him because I could tell that he didn't come from your standard electronic music background.

He came from a more left field spot and I just, and he definitely wasn't interested in being a superstar DJ because you know, when I was growing up in the late nineties, that, that whole world seems pretty like ghost to me and I wasn't interested.

So when I discovered figures like Andrew, I just thought, oh, maybe I could have a spot in this world and just really like inviting, you know, and then when I met him, all of the things I wanted to be true were true.

The fact that he was just genuine and wanted to support new stuff never stopped moving.

You couldn't take your eyes off him because there was a new project of some variety every, seemingly every six months, you know, a new record, a new club.

A new club night, a new idea that he was putting out into the world.

And he was just genuine. I'm going to keep coming back to that word.

It's important for me to say that he never would have wanted to call himself a mentor. Definitely not. He would have been far too humble to say that.

But what I gleaned from him was that, you know, you can't go wrong if you just are yourself. And that's really the only goal.

One thing he would talk about is that trends come and go all the time.

And to follow them is just a force game really. So if you can just be yourself and just do something that feels true to you, then you can't.

It's actually impossible to put a foot wrong. You might be more popular one day than the next, but you're going to leave something behind that you're proud of.

And there's no greater example to me than the weather rule.

[Unclear audio at 00:14:16–00:15:22]

The remix record you've put out too.

What was the decision behind wanting to make a sort of full remix album?

Were there other remix records that inspired you to do that?

Yeah.

Yeah, there were.

I really like it when an artist takes their own work and sort of recontextualizes it.

I think humanly kind of came up with the concept, I guess.

It's definitely an early one, 82, I think.

And The Cure all mixed up is a big one for me.

Nine Inch Nails I've done several over the years.

I loved Massive Attack vs. Mad Professor.

And Soulwax Nite Versions was a huge one for me as a teenager where they took their own rock record and turned it into something more techno-leaning.

That was an enormous record for me.

All of those things really.

I just wanted to, I wasn't going to do it.

There was never a plan to make a club version of it.

But I did a couple and I enjoyed it so much that I just did the whole thing.

And it just really naturally came together.

I'm really happy with it.

It feels like two sides of the same coin for me.

And speaking of influences, are you excited about the new Boards of Canada record on the way?

Were they a big one for you?

Absolutely.

Yeah.

Yeah.

All of that Warp stuff.

Autechre as well.

And obviously Aphex.

Again, just sort of oddball music that sounds kind of alien, but just full of this humanity really.

And hooks and melodies.

And you've managed to create these worlds that you can just get lost inside.

So yeah.

In short, yeah.

I am really excited here.

Well, yeah.

We're really excited that you're going to be bringing your live show to Australia.

Can you tell us a bit about what audiences can expect from you with this one?

I would like to think that if you have enjoyed any corner of my music, there'll be something for you in the live show.

But it's not a DJ set.

You know, there's rave elements to it.

There's huge techno elements to it.

So if you like that side of what I do, you'll definitely find something.

But it also touches upon the guitar-led stuff of what I do.

It's a really intense experience.

There are serene moments, and there are very loud moments.

It's a real, like, short, sharp shock.

And the intensity of a rock show, but with the sort of heartbeat of a techno rave.

I'd say that's probably a more concise way of saying it.

Excellent.

Well, looking forward to you turning Melbourne Town Hall into a big rave room on Saturday the 6th of June.

Thanks heaps for chatting to me, Daniel, today.

Thanks for your time.

Thank you so much.

It's been great.
